_note: Batch 17: restaurants and food supply. Two threads. (1) Restaurant rollups, where the story is concentration and franchise labor terms rather than bankruptcy alone: Roark Capital now controls Subway, Inspire Brands and GoTo Foods, and five of the seven chains that signed the Washington AG's first no-poach assurances in July 2018 were Roark brands. (2) Food supply, where the enforcement record is child labor: Blackstone's Packers Sanitation paid the maximum $1.5M federal penalty for employing 102 children in meat plants, and Charlesbank/Partners Group's Hearthside paid $4.5M to Illinois. Both companies later lost their PE equity to lenders, so both are ownership_status=former. All evidence is business level; no new firm tags, so nothing bleeds across verticals. Panera is placed under the existing JAB Holding record, whose two published firm tags are both veterinary and would otherwise inherit onto the Panera card. batch-18-jab-vet-evidence.json moves them down to Ethos and NVA as business evidence; import it alongside this batch and uncheck publish on the two JAB rows in Firm Tags. New industry values: 'Restaurants' and 'Food processing & supply'. Red Lobster (batch 13) still sits under 'Retail & restaurants'; retag it to 'Restaurants' in Airtable if you want one clean restaurant facet.

firms.notes: Franchise-focused PE firm. Controls Subway, Inspire Brands (Arby's, Buffalo Wild Wings, Sonic, Jimmy John's, Dunkin', Baskin-Robbins) and GoTo Foods (Cinnabon, Auntie Anne's, Jamba, Carvel, Moe's, Schlotzsky's, McAlister's Deli), plus Driven Brands and Primrose Schools outside food.

Restaurant-heavy PE firm. Bought TGI Fridays with Sentinel Capital Partners in 2014 and later took full control; co-owned Hooters of America with Nord Bay Capital from 2019; also an owner of P.F. Chang's. Both TGI Fridays and Hooters filed Chapter 11 and left its hands.

Franchisee holding company controlled by Jay Pandya. Bought Boston Market outright in 2020. Not a conventional PE fund, but the same pattern of a financial owner acquiring an operating chain; included because the labor and vendor record is documented by a state agency and a federal court.

Acquired Hearthside Food Solutions in 2018 alongside Partners Group. Hearthside is a contract manufacturer that packs and bakes for major grocery brands. Lenders took majority ownership through its 2024 bankruptcy.

businesses.platform_company: Franchised sandwich chain, the largest US restaurant chain by store count; taken private by Roark in a reported $9.55B deal

evidence.description: Roark agreed to buy Subway in August 2023 for a reported $9.55B. Because Roark already controlled the sandwich chains Jimmy John's, Arby's, McAlister's Deli and Schlotzsky's, the Federal Trade Commission opened an in-depth antitrust review of the deal in November 2023 rather than clearing it quickly. The FTC ultimately allowed the purchase to proceed without publicly imposed conditions, and the sale closed on April 30, 2024, roughly eight months after it was announced. The result is that one private equity firm now sets franchise terms for Subway alongside Inspire Brands and GoTo Foods.

businesses.business_name: Inspire Brands (Arby's, Buffalo Wild Wings, Dunkin', Sonic, Jimmy John's, Baskin-Robbins)
businesses.platform_company: Roark's restaurant platform, formed in 2018 from the Arby's and Buffalo Wild Wings merger; added Sonic (2018), Jimmy John's (2019) and Dunkin' Brands (December 2020, $11.3B)

evidence.description: On July 12, 2018 the Washington Attorney General announced legally binding assurances of discontinuance, filed in King County Superior Court, requiring seven fast food chains to drop no-poach clauses from their franchise agreements nationwide. No-poach clauses barred a franchisee from hiring a worker away from another franchisee of the same brand, which economists link to suppressed wages for low-paid staff. Three of the seven chains, Arby's, Buffalo Wild Wings and Jimmy John's, were Roark-controlled brands that are now inside Inspire Brands. The AG put the seven chains at more than 25,000 US locations and tens of thousands of affected workers.

businesses.business_name: GoTo Foods (Cinnabon, Auntie Anne's, Jamba, Carvel, Moe's, Schlotzsky's, McAlister's Deli)
businesses.platform_company: Roark's second restaurant platform, built from its 2004 purchase of Cinnabon and known as Focus Brands until it renamed itself GoTo Foods in February 2024

evidence.description: Two of the seven chains covered by the Washington Attorney General's July 12, 2018 no-poach assurances of discontinuance, Cinnabon and Auntie Anne's, were brands of Roark's Focus Brands, now GoTo Foods. The agreements, filed in King County Superior Court, required the franchisors to stop writing no-poach clauses into new franchise agreements and to strike them from existing ones nationwide, not only in Washington. Counting the Inspire brands in the same action, five of the seven chains in the AG's first no-poach announcement were controlled by a single private equity firm.

businesses.platform_company: Bakery-cafe chain bought by JAB for about $7.5B in 2017; held through Panera Brands alongside Caribou Coffee and Einstein Bros. Bagels

evidence.description: Panera faced at least four lawsuits over Charged Lemonade, a self-serve caffeinated drink that contained 390 mg of caffeine in a 30 oz serving without ice, just under the 400 mg daily limit the FDA describes as safe for healthy adults, plus guarana extract. Two suits alleged wrongful death: Sarah Katz, 21, a University of Pennsylvania student with long QT syndrome who died in September 2022, and Dennis Brown, 46, of Florida. Two more alleged lasting cardiac injury. Panera moved the drink behind the counter and added warning signs, then pulled it nationwide in May 2024. It settled the Katz case in October 2024 and the three remaining cases were dismissed with prejudice in July 2025, before trial. Panera denied wrongdoing throughout and no settlement amounts were disclosed.

businesses.platform_company: Casual dining chain bought from Carlson in 2014 for about $890M by TriArtisan and Sentinel Capital Partners; TriArtisan later bought out Sentinel and was majority owner at the bankruptcy filing

evidence.description: Under private equity ownership TGI Fridays shrank from 601 US locations in 2008 to 270 in 2023, a 55 percent decline in restaurants and a 63 percent decline in system-wide sales. A planned sale to the UK-listed Hostmore collapsed, and TGI Fridays Inc. filed Chapter 11 in the Northern District of Texas on November 2, 2024, by then operating only 39 company-owned restaurants and listing assets and liabilities each in the $100M to $500M range. Executive chairman Rohit Manocha attributed the failure to Covid-19 and the company's capital structure. Operating assets went to Mera Global in a Section 363 sale that closed in February 2025, leaving the chain fully franchised and ending TriArtisan's ownership.

businesses.platform_company: Casual dining chain acquired in 2019 by Nord Bay Capital of Tampa and TriArtisan Capital Advisors of New York

evidence.description: After the 2019 buyout by Nord Bay Capital and TriArtisan, sales fell sharply, the pandemic deepened the decline, and the company accumulated more than $300M of debt. Hooters of America filed Chapter 11 in the Northern District of Texas on March 31, 2025 with a restructuring support agreement to sell itself. The buyers were two existing franchisee groups, including the chain's founders, who already ran more than 30 percent of domestic franchised locations. The company exited bankruptcy fully franchisee-owned, and the private equity owners were out.

businesses.platform_company: Rotisserie chicken chain bought in 2020 by Engage Brands, part of Jay Pandya's Rohan Group; store count collapsed from several hundred to a handful

evidence.description: On August 14, 2023 the New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development issued stop-work orders shutting down 27 Boston Market locations statewide. Investigators found $607,471 in back wages owed to 314 workers, and assessed $1,214,942 in liquidated damages, a $182,241.30 administrative fee and $549,500 in administrative penalties, a total of $2,554,154.30 against Boston Chicken of NJ, LLC. The violations included unpaid or late wages, failure to pay minimum wage, failure to pay earned sick leave, records violations and hindering the investigation. The investigation began with a single worker complaint in November 2022. The stores reopened after the company paid more than $630,000 to workers.

Boston Market's owner ran up hundreds of suits from vendors, landlords, franchisors and employees over unpaid bills. The largest, from the food distributor US Foods over unpaid deliveries, ended in a default judgment of about $11.9M after Boston Market failed to defend the case. Jay Pandya later filed for personal bankruptcy. The chain kept operating while the bills went unpaid, so the cost fell first on workers and suppliers.

businesses.platform_company: The largest US contractor for overnight sanitation inside meat and poultry plants; bought by Blackstone Core Equity Partners from Leonard Green & Partners in 2018, renamed Fortrex in January 2025

evidence.description: A US Department of Labor investigation found at least 102 children aged 13 to 17 working overnight sanitation shifts at 13 meat processing plants in eight states, handling caustic cleaning chemicals and cleaning back saws, brisket saws and head splitters. At least three were injured, including chemical burns, and some were falling asleep in school or missing it. Under a federal consent order in Nebraska, PSSI paid $1.5M in civil money penalties, announced February 17, 2023, which was the statutory maximum of $15,138 per minor. The company was also required to hire an outside consultant to run quarterly child labor compliance training for managers. The case triggered a Senate HELP Committee inquiry.

The child labor findings cost the company its customers and eventually its owner. PSSI lost sanitation contracts at Cargill, Tyson Foods and JBS plants in 2023, Moody's downgraded its credit rating in May 2023, and S&P recorded a 14.5 percent year over year revenue drop in the second quarter of 2025. After the company missed a debt payment in October 2025, lenders took control of the equity in an out of court restructuring completed in December 2025, wiping out the Blackstone fund's stake.

businesses.platform_company: One of the largest US contract food manufacturers, packing and baking for major grocery brands; bought in 2018 by Charlesbank Capital Partners and Partners Group, renamed Maker's Pride in March 2025 under lender owners Apollo and Oaktree

evidence.description: A February 2023 New York Times investigation documented migrant children working night shifts in Hearthside plants that made granola bars and packed cereal and snacks. The Illinois Attorney General's office and the Illinois Department of Labor opened a joint investigation and Hearthside agreed to pay $4.5M to settle it, approved by the bankruptcy court on December 6, 2024. The settlement covers people who worked at an Illinois Hearthside facility under the age of 16 between March 1, 2020 and December 4, 2024, and requires state oversight and audits, a reporting hotline and manager training. Hearthside denied violating child labor laws and blamed third-party staffing agencies, whose contracts it says it cut. Federal regulators had separately cited the company for safety violations repeatedly in the preceding five years.

Hearthside filed Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas on November 22, 2024, unable to refinance the debt built up since the 2018 buyout. The plan eliminated more than $1.9B of debt and brought in $200M of new equity at exit, and control passed from Charlesbank and Partners Group to the company's lenders. It emerged in 2025, rebranded as Maker's Pride in March 2025, owned by Apollo and Oaktree.
